title: How to treat depression with AI and a real doctor
summary: Depression treatment online: PHQ-9 screening, SSRI and SNRI medicines, 2026 prices across 6 services, and how a FutureClinic doctor cares by message.
body_markdown:
Treating depression online with a physician involves a clinical evaluation and PHQ-9 symptom screening, followed by a non-controlled antidepressant such as an SSRI, SNRI, bupropion, or mirtazapine if your doctor decides it's right for you, or therapy your doctor can suggest. FutureClinic is not for emergencies: call 911, or call or text 988 (the free, confidential 24/7 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) in a mental-health crisis or if you might hurt yourself or someone else.


Do you want a monthly medication subscription and its requirements, or the same doctor at every follow-up? On FutureClinic, a specific doctor reads your whole case and answers you with a Human Signature, a short video or voice note recorded live for you. No form is approved in bulk. You see physicians only (MD, DO or MBBS), never a nurse practitioner or physician assistant.


Your doctor can also help with other problems in their specialty, such as sleep or thyroid labs. FutureClinic has over 300 doctors. Generalists and specialists practice across more than 60 specialties, and every FutureClinic doctor you see works from one medical record, so different kinds of care sit in one place.


## How do AI and a real doctor work together for depression?


We believe AI is a tool for doctors, and that the technology is not safe enough yet to give medical advice by itself. Depression has nuance and needs one-to-one attention, because only an expert knows when an AI makes a mistake.


On FutureClinic, the doctor is in charge of every case (100% go to a human doctor). FutureClinic's AI works behind the scenes like a chief resident: it gathers your history and prepares a summary you confirm before the doctor reads your case, the whole conversation, and decides. It never gives medical advice by itself. Replies typically come within a few hours, almost always the same day or the next, because real care takes hours, not seconds.


## How is depression recognized and what treatments come first?


According to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), major depressive disorder affects how you feel, think, and handle daily activities; in 2021, 21.0 million US adults (8.3%) had a major depressive episode, and 61.0% got treatment. The US Preventive Services Task Force (June 2023) recommends screening all adults, often with the PHQ-9, which scores nine DSM-5 symptoms from 0 to 3 (5, 10, 15, and 20 mark mild, moderate, moderately severe, and severe depression; 10+ had 88% sensitivity and specificity in a 6,000-patient study) and asks about suicidal thoughts. Diagnosis requires five or more symptoms over two weeks and ruling out causes like low thyroid or vitamin B-12 deficiency (2022 VA/DoD guideline), which your doctor can check with discounted lab tests.


The American College of Physicians (2023 guideline, updated March 2026) suggests cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for mild depression, and CBT or a second-generation antidepressant (or both) for moderate to severe depression. The 2022 VA/DoD guideline recommends therapy or medicine by preference, and suggests both when severe (PHQ-9 above 20), chronic, or recurrent. FutureClinic is not a therapy service, though your doctor can suggest therapy. If your doctor decides it's right for you, they can prescribe a non-controlled first-line antidepressant by message: SSRIs such as sertraline (Zoloft, 50 to 200 mg), escitalopram (Lexapro, 10 to 20 mg), fluoxetine (Prozac), paroxetine (Paxil), and citalopram (Celexa, 20 to 40 mg; 20 mg max over 60 for QT risk); SNRIs such as venlafaxine ER (Effexor XR), duloxetine, and desvenlafaxine (Pristiq); or bupropion XL (Wellbutrin XL, 150 to 300 mg; avoided in seizure or eating disorders), mirtazapine (Remeron, 15 to 45 mg), trazodone, vilazodone (Viibryd), and vortioxetine (Trintellix).


## How long do medicines take, and when is in-person care needed?


NIMH notes antidepressants usually take 4 to 8 weeks to work, often improving sleep and energy before mood. The VA/DoD guideline recommends continuing the full dose for at least six months after remission, and drug labels advise tapering gradually when stopping. Every antidepressant label carries an FDA boxed warning on increased suicidal thoughts and behaviors under age 25 in short-term trials (5 more cases per 1,000 at ages 18 to 24, versus 1 fewer at 25 to 64). Doctors screen for bipolar disorder first and monitor closely early on. Messaging the same doctor on FutureClinic lets your doctor track your PHQ-9 scores and adjust your dose over time.


While AMN Healthcare's 2025 survey found a 31-day average wait for a new-patient physician visit across 15 US metros (23.5 days in family medicine), some cases need in-person or specialist care. VA/DoD guidance directs acute safety risks to emergency or inpatient care, and psychosis, catatonia, or multiple failed trials to specialty care. In-person care is required for rTMS, ECT, and esketamine nasal spray (Spravato, Schedule III). FutureClinic doctors never prescribe controlled medicines, including benzodiazepines (Xanax, Klonopin), stimulants, Spravato, or zuranolone (Zurzuvae, Schedule IV).
